abstract: Octopuses possess highly flexible arms lined with chemo- and mechanosensory suckers that mediate exploration, prey capture, and object manipulation. How individual suckers communicate with adjacent and distant suckers to accomplish such tasks is poorly understood. We developed a behavioral protocol with Octopus bimaculoides to investigate inter-sucker recruitment once an individual sucker encountered an object of interest. We filmed the suckers on individual arms interacting with agarose disks embedded with prey extract and analyzed recruitment dynamics along the two longitudinal rows of suckers on each arm. We observed 18 recruitment patterns involving different sequences of ipsilateral and contralateral suckers. Octopuses most frequently recruited ipsilateral neighboring suckers along the same row, yet many patterns included contralateral suckers in diverse combinations. Recruitment occurred more rapidly toward the arm tip than toward the arm base, and local coordination was ultrafast (mean 155.9 ms between sucker attachments). This directionally organized, ipsilaterally biased, yet flexible recruitment is consistent with distributed neural control along the octopus arm, which may allow octopuses to adapt sucker coordination to the demands of manipulating different items, and may inspire innovation in sucker arrangement and coordination in soft robotic arms.
